entry: Blood relationship between people descended from a common ancestor. Many jurisdictions prohibit marriage or sexual relations between closely related people, although the degree of consanguinity that triggers the prohibition varies. Around 20% of the global population lives in areas where some consanguineous marriages are preferred. Degrees of relationship also determine heirs under intestate succession. In some communities and periods cousin marriage has been allowed or encouraged; in others it is taboo and considered [[Incest|incest]]. Roman civil law, followed by the early canon law of the [[Catholic Church]], barred marriage within four degrees of consanguinity. Around the ninth century the church raised the number to seven and changed how degrees were counted. Consanguinity is illustrated with a consanguinity table, and the Knot System describes it using Ahnentafel numbers of shared ancestors.

Cognitive process of moral judgment based on an individual's values. It produces emotion and rational associations, often felt as remorse when a person acts against their [[Morality|moral values]]. It is distinct from reflexive sensory responses. Debate in modern history has concerned whether conscience should guide moral judgment before an action and whether such judgments should rest on reason. Religious views usually link conscience to a morality inherent in all humans, to a beneficent universe or to divinity. In the [[Upanishads]] and the [[Bhagavad Gita]], it is knowledge of good and evil acquired through [[Karma|karma]] over many lifetimes. In [[Buddhism]] it is linked to a pure heart and a calm mind, and it is regarded as one of the Guardians of the World. Socrates described an inner voice, his daimonic sign, that warned him when he was about to err. Common secular and scientific views hold that the capacity for conscience is probably genetically determined, with its content learned from culture.

Compulsory enlistment in national service, mainly [[Military|military]], enforced by law. Conscription dates to antiquity, but the modern system of near-universal conscription of young men began with the [[French Revolution]] in the 1790s. Most European nations later copied it in peacetime, with men serving one to eight years on active duty before transferring to the reserve. Conscription is controversial on grounds including conscientious objection, opposition to particular wars and sexism, since often only men are subject to the draft. [[Norway]] and [[Sweden]] became the first nations to conscript women on the same legal terms as men in the 2010s, and [[Denmark]] ruled in 2025 to implement a similar system. Many states that have abolished conscription keep the power to reinstate it in wartime. The [[United Kingdom]] abolished conscription in 1960, and it has not been enforced in the [[United States]] since 1973.

Voluntary agreement to the proposal or desires of another. Consent has specific definitions in law, [[Medicine|medicine]], [[Research|research]] and sexual contexts, and it may differ from its everyday meaning. A person with a [[Mental disorder|mental disorder]] or under the legal age of sexual consent may willingly engage in a sexual act that still cannot meet the legal threshold. Consent may be express, unmistakably stated orally, in writing or by a clear gesture, or implied, inferred from actions and circumstances. In medicine, informed consent requires a clear appreciation of the facts, implications and future consequences of an action. Substituted consent allows a decision-maker to establish the decision an incompetent person would have made. Advance consent is generally considered invalid, with exceptions such as healthcare directives. In [[International law|international law]], consent involves states rather than individuals. Under the European General Data Protection Regulation, end-users' consent should be valid, freely given, specific, informed and active.

Class of normative ethical theories that judge conduct by its consequences. An act is right if it will probably produce, or is intended to produce, a greater balance of good over evil than any available alternative. Theories differ in what they count as good, with candidates including [[Pleasure|pleasure]], the absence of pain, the satisfaction of preferences and the general good. [[Utilitarianism]], a prominent variant, is associated with [[Jeremy Bentham]] and [[John Stuart Mill]]. Consequentialism is contrasted with [[Deontology|deontology]], which derives rightness from the character of the act itself, and with virtue ethics, which concerns the character of the agent. G. E. M. Anscombe coined the term in 1958. Critics argue that it can endorse sacrificing an innocent individual if the net outcome is positive, and that it subordinates individual rights to collective gains. Derek Parfit argued that, properly understood, rule consequentialism, Kantian deontology and contractualism would prescribe the same behavior.

Law of physics and chemistry on the conservation of total energy in isolated systems. Energy can be neither created nor destroyed, only transformed or transferred from one form to another. In a closed system, total energy changes only when energy enters or leaves it. When dynamite explodes, chemical energy becomes the [[Kinetic energy|kinetic]] and potential energy of the fragments, heat and sound, and their sum equals the decrease in chemical energy. Classically, energy and mass were treated as separate, but [[Special relativity|special relativity]] links them through [[Mass–energy equivalence|mass–energy equivalence]] (E = mc²), so mass-energy as a whole is conserved. Mass can be converted to energy, as observed in the nuclear binding energy of atomic nuclei. [[Noether's theorem|Noether's theorem]] proves conservation from the continuous time-translation symmetry of physical laws. It follows that a perpetual motion machine of the first kind cannot exist. Depending on how energy is defined, [[General relativity|general relativity]] arguably violates conservation on the cosmological scale.

Scientific law stating that the mass of a closed system remains constant. Mass can be neither created nor destroyed, though it may be rearranged in space or changed in form. In chemical reactions the mass of the reactants equals the mass of the products. Jean Rey demonstrated this in 1630, and [[Antoine Lavoisier]] confirmed it in the late 18th century, a formulation central to the progress from [[Alchemy|alchemy]] to modern [[Chemistry|chemistry]]. The law is widely used in chemistry, mechanics and [[Fluid dynamics|fluid dynamics]], where the continuity equation expresses it. It holds only in the classical limit. In [[General relativity|general relativity]], mass–energy conservation is subject to different definitions, and mass is not generally conserved in open systems.

Jewish religious movement, also known as Masorti Judaism. It regards the authority of Jewish law and tradition as emanating mainly from the assent of the people through the generations, rather than from divine revelation. It views [[Halakha|Halakha]] as both binding and subject to historical development, and it uses modern historical-critical research in matters of practice. It avoids strict theological definitions and allows wide pluralism. Regarding itself as the heir of [[Rabbi|Rabbi]] Zecharias Frankel's 19th-century positive-historical school, it became fully institutionalized in the United States in the mid-20th century. Its largest center is in North America, where the United Synagogue of Conservative Judaism is the main congregational arm and the Jewish Theological Seminary of America is its largest rabbinic seminary. Estimated to represent close to 1.1 million people, including over 600,000 registered adult congregants, it is the third-largest Jewish religious movement worldwide.

British political party of the center-right to right-wing. Founded in 1834 from the Tory Party, it was one of two dominant parties of the 19th century. Under [[Benjamin Disraeli]] it played a preeminent role at the height of the [[British Empire]]. Its rivalry with the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour Party]] has shaped modern British politics. It governed from 2010 to 2024 under five prime ministers, latterly Rishi Sunak. The party has generally favored free markets since the 1980s and is British unionist. It lost the 2024 general election with its lowest vote share ever.

Speech sound articulated with complete or partial closure of the vocal tract. Consonants contrast with vowels. Examples include [p] and [b], pronounced with the lips; [t] and [d], with the front of the tongue; and [f], [v], [s] and [z], forced through a narrow channel (fricatives). Most consonants are pulmonic, using air pressure from the lungs, although a few languages use ejectives, implosives and clicks. The number of speech sounds in the world's languages far exceeds the number of letters in any one [[Alphabet|alphabet]], so linguists devised the [[International Phonetic Alphabet|International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA)]] to give each consonant a unique symbol. English has fewer consonant letters than consonant sounds, so digraphs such as ⟨ch⟩, ⟨sh⟩, ⟨th⟩ and ⟨ng⟩ extend the alphabet. In a [[Syllable|syllable]], consonants typically form the onset and coda around a [[Vowel|vowel]] nucleus.

Explanation of an event invoking a conspiracy when other explanations are more probable. The term has a negative connotation, as such theories are often based on prejudice, emotional conviction, insufficient evidence or paranoia. They resist falsification, because both evidence against them and its absence are read as proof. Belief is linked to distrust of authority and political cynicism, and psychologists have associated it with paranoia, narcissism and insecure attachment. Historically, conspiracy theories have been closely linked to prejudice, [[Propaganda|propaganda]], witch hunts, wars and [[Genocide|genocides]]. AIDS denialism by the government of [[South Africa]] caused an estimated 330,000 deaths from AIDS. Beliefs about genetically modified foods led the government of [[Zambia]] to reject food aid during a famine, when three million people in the country were suffering from hunger. Conspiracy theories also obstruct public health measures such as [[Vaccination|vaccination]]. Interventions include maintaining an open society, encouraging analytical thinking and reducing feelings of uncertainty, anxiety or powerlessness.

Romanian sculptor, painter and photographer. Regarded as one of the most influential sculptors of the 20th century and a pioneer of [[Modernism|modernism]], he is called the patriarch of modern sculpture. Born in the village of Hobița, he displayed as a child an aptitude for carving wooden farm tools. Formal studies took him to [[Bucharest|Bucharest]], [[Munich|Munich]] and the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris (1905–07). His art emphasizes clean geometrical lines that balance the forms inherent in his materials with symbolic allusion. It drew on Romanian folk art, and like [[Paul Gauguin|Paul Gauguin]] and [[Pablo Picasso|Pablo Picasso]], he sought inspiration in non-European cultures as a source of primitive exoticism.

City (pop. about 450,000), capital of Constantine Province, northeastern [[Algeria|Algeria]]. Located about 80 km inland from the Mediterranean coast on the Rhumel River, it is regarded as the commercial center of eastern Algeria. With 938,475 people including its agglomeration, it is the third-largest city in the country after [[Algiers|Algiers]] and [[Oran|Oran]]. Known as the City of Bridges for the bridges that connect its hills and ravines, it was the Berber Numidian capital Cirta, and in 112 BC the Numidian king Jugurtha ruled from it. It was rebuilt in 313 AD and renamed Constantina after [[Constantine the Great|Constantine the Great]]. Captured by the [[Vandals|Vandals]] in 432, it became known as Qacentina after the Arab conquest of the 8th century. In 2015 it was named the Arab Capital of Culture.

Greek poet, journalist and civil servant. Born in [[Alexandria|Alexandria]], he is sometimes considered the most distinguished Greek [[Poetry|poet]] of the 20th century. His poetic canon consists of 154 poems, and his work has contributed importantly to Western poetry as a whole. He refused to publish books, preferring to share his work through [[Newspaper|newspapers]] and [[Magazine|magazines]] or to print it himself on broadsheets. His most important poems were written after his fortieth birthday and published two years after his death. E. M. Forster introduced his poems to the English-speaking world in 1923, describing him as "a Greek gentleman in a straw hat, standing absolutely motionless at a slight angle to the universe."

Roman emperor (r. 306–337). The first Roman emperor to convert to [[Christianity|Christianity]], he played a pivotal role in elevating the religion's status. The Edict of Milan in 313 legalized Christianity in the [[Roman Empire|Roman Empire]]. He served under [[Diocletian|Diocletian]] and was proclaimed *augustus* by his army at York after his father's death in 306. He became sole ruler in 324. He introduced the solidus, a gold coin that became the standard for Byzantine and European currencies for more than a thousand years. He founded [[Constantinople|Constantinople]] on the site of Byzantium as the new capital. He convoked the [[First Council of Nicaea|First Council of Nicaea]] in 325, which produced the Nicene Creed. Historians debate his beliefs, and he is venerated as a saint in Eastern Christianity and parts of Western Christianity.

Former imperial capital, now Istanbul, Turkey. Founded on the site of Byzantium in 324 by [[Constantine the Great|Constantine the Great]] as Nova Roma, it became the eastern capital of the [[Roman Empire|Roman Empire]] in 330 and remained its sole capital after the western parts were lost in the 5th century. From the mid-5th to the early 13th century it was the largest and wealthiest city in Europe. Its walls held off besiegers for nearly nine hundred years, and the [[Hagia Sophia|Hagia Sophia]] cathedral was among its famous buildings. It was sacked by Crusaders in 1204 and conquered by the [[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman Empire]] in 1453. It remained the Ottoman capital until the Republic of Turkey moved the capital to [[Ankara|Ankara]] in 1923. It is now the most populous city in Europe, with more than 16 million residents.

Area of the [[Celestial sphere|celestial sphere]] containing a group of stars that forms a perceived pattern or outline. Constellations typically represent animals, mythological subjects or objects. The first were probably defined in prehistory, and many cultures invented their own, some of which changed in size or shape or fell out of use. Twelve or thirteen ancient constellations of the [[Zodiac|zodiac]] straddle the [[Ecliptic|ecliptic]]; astrological divisions of the zodiac became prominent around 400 BC in Babylonian astronomy. [[Ptolemy|Ptolemy]] listed 48 constellations in the *Almagest*. In 1922 the International Astronomical Union accepted a modern list of 88 constellations, and in 1928 it adopted boundaries covering the entire celestial sphere. Asterisms such as the [[Big Dipper|Big Dipper]] in [[Ursa Major|Ursa Major]] are informal star patterns, not formal constellations.

Supreme legal document of India and the longest written national constitution in the world. Adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 26 November 1949 and effective from 26 January 1950, it establishes a sovereign, socialist, secular and democratic [[Republic|republic]], sets out fundamental rights, directive principles and citizens' duties. It is based largely on the Government of India Act 1935 and asserts constitutional supremacy rather than parliamentary supremacy. The Supreme Court has held that certain basic features cannot be removed by amendment. India celebrates the constitution on 26 January as Republic Day.

Supreme law of the United States of America. It superseded the Articles of Confederation on March 4, 1789. Drafted at the Constitutional Convention in [[Philadelphia|Philadelphia]], which met from May 25 to September 17, 1787, it was influenced by [[Common law|English common law]] and the liberalism of [[John Locke|John Locke]] and [[Montesquieu|Montesquieu]]. Its first three articles embody the [[Separation of powers|separation of powers]] among a bicameral Congress, the president and the judiciary. Articles IV, V and VI embody [[Federalism|federalism]], addressing state relations and amendment. It has been amended 27 times. The first ten amendments, the Bill of Rights, protect individual liberty and restrict government power. Amendments 13–15 are the Reconstruction Amendments. It is the oldest and longest-standing written and codified national constitution in force, and it has influenced the constitutions of other nations.

Form of monarchy in which the monarch shares decisions under a constitution. Also called limited, parliamentary or democratic monarchy, it differs from an [[Absolute monarchy|absolute monarchy]], in which the monarch alone decides. The monarch is bound to act within an established legal framework and is often a visible symbol of national unity. Some monarchs are largely ceremonial heads of state, while others hold formal powers such as veto, appointment and the power to dissolve parliament. In [[Liechtenstein|Liechtenstein]], [[Monaco|Monaco]], [[Morocco|Morocco]], [[Jordan|Jordan]], Kuwait, Bahrain, Thailand and Bhutan, the constitution grants substantial discretionary powers to the sovereign. In the [[United Kingdom|United Kingdom]], Spain, Sweden, Norway, Japan and other Commonwealth realms, the monarch retains significantly less personal discretion. Malaysia and Cambodia are elective monarchies, in which a small electoral college periodically selects the ruler. Many constitutional monarchies are democratic, but some are not.

Electronic devices intended for everyday household use, mainly for entertainment, communication and recreation. Historically known as black goods in American English, because many were housed in dark casings, and brown goods in British English, they are distinguished from white goods such as washing machines and [[Refrigerator|refrigerators]]. The first major product was the broadcast receiver, from the early 20th century [[Radio broadcasting|radio broadcasting]]. Later products included [[Telephone|telephones]], [[Television|televisions]], [[Calculator|calculators]], [[Camera|cameras]], [[Video game console|video game consoles]] and [[Mobile phone|mobile phones]]. Video equipment progressed from VCRs in the 1980s and 1990s to DVD and Blu-ray players. Since the 2010s most products have been digital and have merged with the computer and video game industries, a trend called the consumerization of information technology. Modern products include virtual reality goggles, smart home devices and wearable technology.

Receptacle or enclosure for holding an item. Things kept inside a container are protected on several sides by its structure. Containers are used for storage, packaging and transportation, including shipping, and the term is most often applied to durable, partly or wholly rigid devices. A container can also be considered a basic [[Tool|tool]]. Humans have used containers for at least 100,000 years, and possibly for millions of years. The first containers were probably invented for storing [[Food|food]], which allowed early humans to preserve it longer, carry it more easily and protect it from other animals. The development of food storage containers was of immense importance to evolving human populations and was a totally innovative behavior not seen in other primates.

Art created from the 1970s onward. Contemporary artists work in a globally influenced, culturally diverse and technologically advancing world, continuing the challenge to boundaries that was already well under way in the 20th century. It is distinguished by the lack of any uniform organizing principle, ideology or -ism. It engages with personal and cultural identity, family, community and nationality. In English, modern and contemporary are synonyms, which causes confusion between [[Modern art|modern art]] and contemporary art by non-specialists. Some specialists consider the frontier between the two blurry; the French Musée National d'Art Moderne does not differentiate them in its collections.

European art music composed close to the present day. At the beginning of the 21st century the term commonly referred to post-1945 post-tonal music after the death of Anton Webern, including serial, [[Electronic music|electronic]], experimental and [[Minimalism|minimalist]] music. Newer forms include spectral music and post-minimalism. After [[World War I|World War I]], neoclassical composers sought to recapture the balanced forms of earlier styles as a reaction against late [[Romanticism|Romanticism]]. Postwar modernists pursued greater control through the twelve-tone technique and total serialism, while others explored indeterminacy and aleatoric processes. Technological advances led to electronic music, and experiments with tape loops and repetitive textures contributed to the advent of minimalism.

Subset of modern history, in English-language historiography, covering the period from about 1945 to the present. It is politically dominated by the [[Cold War|Cold War]] between the Western Bloc, led by the United States, and the [[Eastern Bloc|Eastern Bloc]], led by the Soviet Union, which raised fears of nuclear war. Both sides intervened in smaller nations through proxy wars. The Cold War ended with the [[Revolutions of 1989|Revolutions of 1989]] and the [[Dissolution of the Soviet Union|dissolution of the Soviet Union]] in 1991. [[Decolonization|Decolonization]] created new states in Southeast Asia, the Middle East and Africa between 1945 and 1975. The first supranational organizations, such as the United Nations, emerged after 1945. The [[Sexual revolution|sexual revolution]] transformed social relations in Western countries between the 1960s and 1980s. Japan and [[West Germany|West Germany]] emerged as exceptionally strong economies, and [[Globalization|globalization]] led to new financial and industrial centers in Asia.
